questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System
questions.stem: The bilaminar embryo shown develops a primitive streak and primitive node. What key process do these structures initiate?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neurulation - closure of the neural tube

explanation.summary: Epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to generate endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm during gastrulation. The primitive node organizes the body axis; neural tube closure (neurulation) occurs afterward.
explanation.whyCorrect: Epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to generate endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm during gastrulation. The primitive node organizes the body axis; neural tube closure (neurulation) occurs afterward.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fertilization occurs in the ampulla before cleavage, days before a bilaminar disc or primitive streak exists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neurulation follows gastrulation; the notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate after the streak has generated three germ layers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Placental villi form from trophoblast (syncytio- and cytotrophoblast) with extraembryonic mesoderm; the primitive streak is an embryonic disc structure that makes germ layers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Implantation of the blastocyst occurs in the second week, before the bilaminar disc develops a primitive streak in the third week.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System
questions.stem: The developing embryo shown forms pharyngeal (branchial) arches and pouches. The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to which primary lymphoid organ?

explanation.summary: The third pharyngeal pouch forms the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. Failure of third/fourth pouch development causes DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia with T-cell deficiency and hypocalcemia).
explanation.whyCorrect: The third pharyngeal pouch forms the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. Failure of third/fourth pouch development causes DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia with T-cell deficiency and hypocalcemia).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bursa of Fabricius is the avian B-cell organ derived from the cloaca; humans have no bursa, and the third pouch forms the thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The spleen develops from mesenchyme in the dorsal mesogastrium, not from a pharyngeal pouch, and it is a secondary lymphoid organ.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bone marrow is a primary lymphoid organ, but it arises within developing bones from mesoderm, not from pharyngeal pouch endoderm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The palatine tonsil derives from the second pharyngeal pouch and is a secondary lymphoid organ, not the third-pouch derivative.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System
questions.stem: The right-hand histology section shows an organ with an outer cortex, an inner medulla, and eosinophilic whorled keratinized structures within the medulla. Which organ is this?

explanation.summary: The whorled eosinophilic Hassall's corpuscles in the medulla are characteristic of the thymus, where developing T cells undergo positive selection (cortex) and negative selection (medulla). The left diagram shows its pharyngeal arch/pouch origin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The whorled eosinophilic Hassall's corpuscles in the medulla are characteristic of the thymus, where developing T cells undergo positive selection (cortex) and negative selection (medulla). The left diagram shows its pharyngeal arch/pouch origin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A lymph node has a cortex with follicles, a paracortex and medullary cords and sinuses, but no Hassall's corpuscles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The spleen is organized into white pulp (periarteriolar sheaths and follicles) and red pulp with sinusoids, not cortex and medulla with keratinized whorls.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The parathyroid gland consists of chief and oxyphil cells in cords with fat; it lacks lymphoid cortex and medulla and has no Hassall's corpuscles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The palatine tonsil is covered by stratified squamous epithelium with deep crypts and lymphoid follicles; it lacks a cortex-medulla arrangement with Hassall's corpuscles.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System
questions.stem: This graph of infant serum immunoglobulins shows a transient dip in IgG at roughly 3-6 months of age. What causes this physiologic nadir?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A Bruton tyrosine kinase mutation blocking all B-cell development

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of maternal IgA from breast milk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal transplacental IgG has been catabolized

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymic aplasia (DiGeorge syndrome) preventing T-cell help

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autoantibody-mediated destruction of infant plasma cells

explanation.summary: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects the newborn, then declines over the first months of life. Because the infant's own IgG synthesis ramps up more slowly, a transient physiologic hypogammaglobulinemia appears around 3-6 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects the newborn, then declines over the first months of life. Because the infant's own IgG synthesis ramps up more slowly, a transient physiologic hypogammaglobulinemia appears around 3-6 months.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BTK mutation (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) causes persistent absence of B cells and all immunoglobulins, not a transient physiologic dip that recovers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Breast-milk IgA acts locally in the gut and is not absorbed to raise serum IgG; the dip shown is in serum IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DiGeorge syndrome is a pathologic thymic defect with hypocalcemia and T-cell deficiency; the 3-6 month IgG nadir occurs in every healthy infant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no autoantibody destruction of infant plasma cells; the nadir reflects normal catabolism of maternal IgG before the infant's own production rises.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System
questions.stem: In the postnatal gut mucosa shown, the lumen is defended by secretory antibody even before the infant's own mucosal immunity matures. What is the major source of this early protective secretory IgA?

explanation.summary: Secretory IgA in breast milk and colostrum coats the neonatal gut mucosa, providing passive mucosal immunity. M cells overlying Peyer's patches sample luminal antigen, but the infant's own robust secretory IgA production develops only over the first months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secretory IgA in breast milk and colostrum coats the neonatal gut mucosa, providing passive mucosal immunity. M cells overlying Peyer's patches sample luminal antigen, but the infant's own robust secretory IgA production develops only over the first months.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transplacental transfer carries maternal IgG via FcRn, not IgA; secretory IgA does not cross the placenta.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fetal plasma cells produce little immunoglobulin, and mucosal secretory IgA comes from plasma cells in the lamina propria, which matures only over the first months.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complement-derived opsonins such as C3b are not antibodies and are not secreted onto the gut lumen as secretory IgA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paneth cells secrete defensins, lysozyme and phospholipase A2, not IgA; IgA is made by lamina propria plasma cells and transported by epithelial poly-Ig receptor.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System
questions.stem: This graph tracks the site of hematopoiesis across gestation. Which organ is the predominant site of blood-cell production during the middle of fetal development (around months 4-6)?

explanation.summary: Hematopoiesis begins in the yolk sac, shifts to the fetal liver (with a brief splenic contribution) in mid-gestation, then moves to the bone marrow, which becomes the definitive site by birth and remains so in adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hematopoiesis begins in the yolk sac, shifts to the fetal liver (with a brief splenic contribution) in mid-gestation, then moves to the bone marrow, which becomes the definitive site by birth and remains so in adults.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone marrow becomes dominant only in the last trimester and after birth; at months 4-6 the liver is the main site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymph nodes are not a significant site of fetal hematopoiesis; they host lymphocyte responses rather than producing the full range of blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The yolk sac is the earliest site, in roughly the first 2 months, and has largely ceded production to the liver by mid-gestation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymus is where T cells mature, not a general site of blood-cell production during fetal life.

questions.topicName: Effect of Age on the Immune System
questions.stem: This schematic traces the origin of long-lived tissue-resident macrophages (such as microglia, alveolar, and skin macrophages). What is their principal embryonic source?

explanation.summary: Many tissue-resident macrophages arise from yolk-sac and fetal-liver progenitors during embryogenesis and maintain themselves by local self-renewal, largely independent of adult bone-marrow-derived monocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many tissue-resident macrophages arise from yolk-sac and fetal-liver progenitors during embryogenesis and maintain themselves by local self-renewal, largely independent of adult bone-marrow-derived monocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adult bone-marrow monocytes replenish some macrophage populations (e.g., gut, dermis) and inflammatory macrophages, but long-lived microglia and alveolar macrophages self-renew from embryonic precursors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thymic epithelial cells derive from third-pouch endoderm and support T-cell selection; they are not hematopoietic and do not give rise to macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neural crest gives rise to melanocytes, peripheral neurons, Schwann cells and craniofacial structures; macrophages are hematopoietic, including microglia from yolk-sac progenitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marginal-zone B cells are lymphocytes that make rapid antibody against blood-borne antigens; they do not differentiate into tissue macrophages.
